docs.title: Mapping Entry Points and Bootstrapping Sequences
docs.text:
• In raw PHP applications, execution always begins at a specific file hit directly by the web server (or CLI script).
    [ Incoming HTTP Request ]
               │
               ▼
        ┌─────────────┐
        │ .htaccess / │ (URL Rewriting)
        │  Nginx.conf │
        └──────┬──────┘
               │
               ▼
        ┌─────────────┐
        │  index.php  │ (Front Controller Entry)
        └──────┬──────┘
               │
               ▼
        ┌─────────────┐
        │  bootstrap  │ (Autoloaders, Configs, DB Singletons, Error Handlers)
        └──────┬──────┘
               │
               ▼
        ┌─────────────┐
        │ Router /    │ (URI Dispatching)
        │ Dispatcher  │
        └──────┬──────┘
               │
               ▼
        ┌─────────────┐
        │ Controller  │ (Business Logic & Active Record DB Operations)
        └─────────────┘

docs.title: Identify the Entry Point Pattern
docs.text:
• Raw PHP projects generally follow one of two execution entry models.
  • Front Controller Pattern (Single Entry)
    • All requests redirect to a single file (usually public/index.php or index.php).
  • Legacy Script-per-Page Pattern (Multi-Entry)
    • Every endpoint corresponds to a physical script (e.g., api/get_user.php, api/update_order.php).

docs.title: Trace the Bootstrapping Order
docs.text:
• Regardless of entry model, locate the bootstrap sequence at the top of the file.
  • Look for require, require_once, include, or include_once calls in the first lines.

docs.title: Tracing Dependencies and Singleton Instances
docs.text: • In raw PHP codebases, dependency management relies on Singletons, Static Service Locators, or Registry Patterns rather than automated Dependency Injection containers like those found in Symfony or Laravel.

docs.title: The Singleton Pattern
docs.text: • Used to ensure a single shared instance (such as a database connection pool or configuration loader) exists across the entire request lifecycle.

docs.title: The Global Registry / Service Locator
docs.text:
• Used in legacy systems to store global instances in an associative array or static container.
class AppRegistry {
    private static array $services = [];

    public static function set(string $key, object $service): void {
        self::$services[$key] = $service;
    }

    public static function get(string $key): object {
        if (!isset(self::$services[$key])) {
            throw new Exception("Service {$key} not registered.");
        }
        return self::$services[$key];
    }
}

// Bootstrap initialization:
AppRegistry::set('db_writer', new PDO(...));
AppRegistry::set('db_reader', new PDO(...));

// Retrieval inside custom ORM:
$writer = AppRegistry::get('db_writer');

docs.title: Globals Array Interception
docs.text:
• In older raw PHP applications, shared instances are stored directly inside PHP's native $GLOBALS superglobal array.
// In bootstrap script:
$GLOBALS['db'] = new CustomDatabaseWrapper();

// Deep inside a model file:
function fetchUser(int $id) {
    global $db; // Pulls instance from $GLOBALS['db']
    // OR
    $db = $GLOBALS['db'];
    return $db->query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {$id}");
}

docs.title: Locating Configurations and Environment Variables
docs.text:
• Configurations in raw PHP projects generally load through one of three mechanisms.
  • Dotenv Parser Libraries (vlucas/phpdotenv)
    • If the project uses Composer, it likely parses a .env file into PHP's runtime environment ($_ENV and getenv()).
  • Arrays Returning Configuration Files
    • Common in structured custom frameworks.
    • Configuration files in a config/ directory return PHP arrays directly.
  • Legacy Constant Definitions
    • Found in older raw PHP applications.
    • Configurations are defined as global constants during the bootstrap phase.

docs.title: Data Access
docs.text: All content here was generated by Gemini.

docs.title: PHP Data Objects Core
docs.text:
• PDO is the standard native database abstraction layer in modern PHP applications.
  • It provides a uniform interface for database interaction, enforces prepared statements, and isolates lower-level driver mechanics.

docs.title: Establishing PDO connections
docs.text:
• A PDO instance is created by passing a Data Source Name (DSN), database username, password, and driver configuration options to its constructor.
  • Data Source Name (DSN) format consists of the driver prefix (e.g., mysql:), followed by database host, name, port, and character encoding parameters separated by semicolons.
  • Character Set Specification: Setting charset=utf8mb4 inside the DSN guarantees UTF-8 handling at the connection level, preventing Unicode conversion exploits.
  • Connection Error Leakage: Instantiating PDO directly inside try-catch blocks is required to prevent raw stack traces from exposing database credentials in unhandled exception output.
  • Native Emulation (PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES)
    • When true (default in older PHP versions), PDO emulates prepared statements natively in PHP before sending raw SQL strings to MySQL.
    • When false, PDO sends actual prepared statements to MySQL via the binary protocol, forcing the database engine to parse and compile the SQL template independently of runtime parameters.
<?php
$dsn = 'mysql:host=rds-primary.c123456.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com;dbname=app_db;port=3306;charset=utf8mb4';
$username = 'db_user';
$password = 'secret_pass';

$options = [
    PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE            => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,
    PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
    PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES   => false,
];

try {
    $pdo = new PDO($dsn, $username, $password, $options);
} catch (PDOException $e) {
    // Exception message contains sensitive host/credential information
}
>

docs.title: Prepared statements and Parameter binding
docs.text:
• Prepared statements separate SQL compilation from execution, rendering parameter payload values incapable of altering SQL query structure.
  • Positional Placeholders (?) 
    <?php
$sql = "SELECT id, email, status FROM users WHERE status = ? AND created_at >= ?";
$stmt = $pdo->prepare($sql);

$stmt->execute(['active', '2026-01-01 00:00:00']);
$users = $stmt->fetchAll();
>
  • Named Placeholders (:name)
    • bindValue() passes the value directly at the moment of binding.
    • bindParam() binds by reference (&$variable), evaluating the value only when $stmt->execute() is invoked.
    • Using bindParam() inside loops without careful variable management can introduce unexpected state mutation bugs. 
      <?php
$sql = "SELECT id, email, status FROM users WHERE status = :status AND created_at >= :created_at";
$stmt = $pdo->prepare($sql);

// Explicit binding with data types
$stmt->bindValue(':status', 'active', PDO::PARAM_STR);
$stmt->bindValue(':created_at', '2026-01-01 00:00:00', PDO::PARAM_STR);
$stmt->execute();
>

docs.title: Fetch modes
docs.text:
• Fetch modes determine how query result rows are structured in memory.
  • PDO::FETCH_ASSOC returns an array indexed by column name.
  • PDO::FETCH_OBJ returns an anonymous stdClass object with property names matching SQL result set columns.
  • PDO::FETCH_CLASS instantiates instances of a specified class, mapping columns directly to class properties before calling the class constructor.
  • FETCH_CLASS Property Assignment Ordering:
    • PDO hydrates properties before invoking __construct().
    • If class property defaults are declared in code, constructor assignments will overwrite values hydrated by PDO during execution.
<?php
class UserEntity {
    public int $id;
    public string $username;
    public string $email;
}


$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT id, username, email FROM users WHERE id = :id");
$stmt->execute([':id' => 42]);

$row = $stmt->fetch(PDO::FETCH_ASSOC);
// Output: ['id' => 42, 'username' => 'alex', 'email' => 'alex@example.com']

$row = $stmt->fetch(PDO::FETCH_OBJ);
// Output: $row->id (42), $row->username ('alex')


$stmt->setFetchMode(PDO::FETCH_CLASS, UserEntity::class);
$user = $stmt->fetch(); // $user is an instance of UserEntity
>

docs.title: Error Handling Modes (PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE)
docs.text:
• PDO::ERRMODE_SILENT (Legacy Default): Sets error codes silently. Requires manual checking of $pdo->errorCode() or $stmt->errorInfo().
  • PDO::ERRMODE_WARNING: Emits a PHP runtime E_WARNING while continuing script execution.
  • PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION (Modern Standard): Throws a PDOException on any database failure, allowing block transaction management.

docs.title: Transaction Control
docs.text:
• DDL commands trigger implicit transaction commits in MySQL.
  • Enclosing DDL queries inside PDO transactions will break rollback functionality.
<?php
// sample transaction handling
try {
    $pdo->beginTransaction();

    $stmt1 = $pdo->prepare("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amount WHERE id = :from");
    $stmt1->execute([':amount' => 100, ':from' => 1]);

    $stmt2 = $pdo->prepare("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + :amount WHERE id = :to");
    $stmt2->execute([':amount' => 100, ':to' => 2]);

    $pdo->commit();
} catch (PDOException $e) {
    if ($pdo->inTransaction()) {
        $pdo->rollBack();
    }
    throw $e;
}
>

docs.title: Deconstructing the Active Record Pattern
docs.text:
• The Active Record architectural pattern maps a database table or view to a class, and an individual database row to an instance of that class.

  • Single Responsibility Dual Role: An Active Record instance carries both business domain data (row attributes) and database persistence behavior (save(), delete(), update()).

    Database Table: `users`               PHP Class Definition: `User`
+----+----------+-----------------+   +--------------------------------+
| id | name     | email           |   | class User extends Model { ... }|
+----+----------+-----------------+   +--------------------------------+
|  1 | Alice    | alice@test.com  |  ---> $user1 = new User(); (Row 1)
|  2 | Bob      | bob@test.com    |  ---> $user2 = new User(); (Row 2)
+----+----------+-----------------+

  • Rather than declaring static public class properties for every database table column, custom Active Record implementations intercept reads and writes using internal key-value storage.

    <?php
abstract class ActiveRecord {
    protected array $attributes = [];
    protected array $original = [];

    public function __construct(array $attributes = []) {
        $this->fill($attributes);
    }

    public function fill(array $attributes): void {
        foreach ($attributes as $key => $value) {
            $this->__set($key, $value);
        }
    }

    public function __get(string $key): mixed {
        // Support custom getter mutators (e.g., getFirstNameAttribute)
        $mutator = 'get' . $this->studly($key) . 'Attribute';
        if (method_exists($this, $mutator)) {
            return $this->$mutator();
        }

        return $this->attributes[$key] ?? null;
    }

    public function __set(string $key, mixed $value): void {
        // Support custom setter mutators (e.g., setPasswordAttribute)
        $mutator = 'set' . $this->studly($key) . 'Attribute';
        if (method_exists($this, $mutator)) {
            $this->$mutator($value);
            return;
        }

        $this->attributes[$key] = $value;
    }

    protected function studly(string $value): string {
        return str_replace(' ', '', ucwords(str_replace(['-', '_'], ' ', $value)));
    }
}
>

  • To avoid generating unnecessary update queries that overwrite unchanged columns, active record models maintain an internal record of original attributes populated during database hydration.

docs.title: Dissecting Custom Database Wrappers
docs.text:
• Custom frameworks implement proprietary abstraction wrappers around PDO to provide fluid query building, model hydration, relation handling, and connection management.
  • Query Builders accumulate SQL fragments inside private array properties and assemble a complete, parameter-bound SQL string upon calling terminal methods like get() or first().
  • Custom Active Record implementations resolve associations either through dynamic methods that execute secondary queries, or by auto-generating join clauses.
  • Invoking relationship methods inside loops (e.g., looping through 100 posts and executing $post->author() on each iteration) executes \(N+1\) discrete database queries.
  • Code bases address this via manual eager loading implementations (WHERE IN (...)).
  • Production setups with AWS RDS utilize an Amazon RDS Writer Endpoint (Primary DB) alongside one or more Reader Endpoints (Read Replicas).
  • Custom database abstraction layers manage connection splitting to route traffic efficiently and offload read execution.

docs.title: Data Types & Type Juggling
docs.text: This section focuses on how PHP interprets data under the hood, how legacy implicit type conversions cause hidden bugs, and how modern PHP type signatures clarify code intent.

docs.title: Built-in Types
docs.text: PHP has eight primary primitive/built-in types divided into standard categories.

docs.title: Scalar Types (Single-value containers)
docs.text:
• bool
    • true or false
    • case-insensitive in raw PHP: TRUE, False.
  • int
    • Whole numbers (e.g., 42, -10).
    • On 64-bit systems, PHP_INT_MAX is \(2^{63}-1\).
  • float
    • Also historically called double
    • Floating-point numbers (e.g., 3.14, 1.0).

  • string

    • Series of characters.
    • Strings can be enclosed in single quotes ('...') or double quotes ("...").
    • Double-quoted strings support variable interpolation.
    <?php
$id = 45;
$sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $id"; // Variable $id expands to 45
$sql = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $id'; // Literal string, no expansion
>

docs.title: Compound Types
docs.text:
• array

    • In PHP, an array is actually an ordered map, it maps keys to values.
    • It acts as a list, hash map, dictionary, stack, and queue all at once.
    <?php
// Modern short array syntax (PHP 5.4+)
$user = ['id' => 1, 'name' => 'Alice'];

// Legacy array syntax (Very common in older code bases)
$user = array('id' => 1, 'name' => 'Alice');
>

  • object

    • Instance of a class.
  • callable
    • A reference to something that can be invoked as a function.
    • Strings naming a function, or arrays like [$instance, 'methodName'].

docs.title: Special Types
docs.text:
• null
    • Represents a variable with no value.
    • A variable is null if it has been assigned the constant NULL, has not been initialized yet, or was unset().
  • resource
    • Holds a reference to an external resource (e.g., an open database connection, a file handle returned by fopen()).

docs.title: Strict and Weak Typing, Type Juggling
docs.text:
• PHP is traditionally a dynamically and weakly typed language.
  • It does not require to declare variable types explicitly when creating variables (e.g., $x = 10;).
  • Type Juggling is PHP's automatic conversion of data types depending on the context in which an expression is evaluated.
  • By default, PHP operates in Weak Typing Mode.
  • If a function expects an int and calling method passes the string "123", PHP coerces it to 123 silently.
  • Modern PHP (7.0+) allows developers to enforce Strict Typing Mode on a per-file basis using a directive at the top of the file.
    • This only affects function calls made from within that specific file.
    • If File A (without strict types) calls a function declared in File B (which has strict types), the call is evaluated in weak mode (File A's setting governs the call site).
    • It strictly checks int, float, string, and bool.
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function setAge(int $age) {
    return "Age set to " . $age;
}

setAge(30);     // Works fine
setAge("30");   // Throws a TypeError when strict_types=1 is active
>

docs.title: Common Automatic Conversions
docs.text:
• String to Numeric Expressions: If an operator expects a number (like +), PHP converts strings to numbers. 
    <?php
$total = "10" + 20;     // Result: (int) 30
$total = "10.5" + 20;   // Result: (float) 30.5

// PHP 7.x Legacy Behavior (PHP 8 throws a TypeError or Warning):
$total = "10 apples" + 5; // Result: (int) 15 (Extracts leading numeric part)
>
  • Truthy and Falsy Evaluations:
    • In conditional checks (if ($var)), PHP casts values to boolean automatically.
  • Loose Comparison vs. Strict Comparison
    • == (Equal): Checks value after type juggling.
    • === (Identical): Checks value and type without conversion.

docs.title: Basic Parameter and Return Type Declarations (PHP 7.0+)
docs.text:
• Function signatures can explicitly declare input parameters and return types. 
    <?php
function calculateTax(float $amount, float $rate): float {
    return $amount * $rate;
}
>

docs.title: Nullable Types (?Type) (PHP 7.1+)
docs.text:
• By default, typed parameters/returns do not accept null.
  • Prefixing a type with ? makes it explicit that null is a valid value. 
    <?php
// $user can be an instance of User OR null
// Returns a string OR null
function getUsername(?User $user): ?string {
    if ($user === null) {
        return null;
    }
    return $user->name;
}
>

docs.title: Union Types (TypeA|TypeB) (PHP 8.0+)
docs.text:
• Allows a variable, parameter, or return value to accept multiple distinct types. 
    <?php
class UserRepository {
    // $id can be an integer (12) or string UUID ("a1b2-c3d4")
    public function findUser(int|string $id): User|false {
        // Query database...
        if (!$found) {
            return false; // Very common legacy pattern: return false on failure
        }
        return $user;
    }
}
>

docs.title: Specialized Types
docs.text:
• mixed: Equivalent to array|bool|callable|int|float|object|resource|string|null. Means "any value."
  • void: Indicates a function performs an action but returns no value (using return; or returning nothing).
  • never: Indicates a function never terminates normally (it either calls exit(), die(), or throws an Exception).

docs.title: Indexed vs. Associative arrays
docs.text: Unlike languages with distinct List, Map, or Dictionary types, PHP uses a single array type that acts as an ordered hash map.

docs.title: Indexed Arrays
docs.text:
• Keys are automatically assigned integers starting at 0 unless specified otherwise.
  • Deleting an item with unset($array[1]) does not re-index the remaining items. The array becomes [0 => 'a', 2 => 'c'].
<?php
$statuses = ['active', 'pending', 'inactive'];

// Behind the scenes, PHP stores this as:
// [0 => 'active', 1 => 'pending', 2 => 'inactive']
>

docs.title: Associative Arrays
docs.text:
• Keys are custom strings or custom integers.
  • This is how raw database rows and JSON payloads are represented when converted to PHP.
  • PHP allows mixing integer and string keys in the same array.
  • PHP automatically converts numeric string keys to integers.
<?php
$user = [
    'id' => 42,
    'email' => 'alex@example.com',
    'role' => 'admin',
    '10' => 'A', // Key '10' is silently cast to integer 10
    10   => 'B'  // Overwrites the key 10! Value is now 'B'
];
>

docs.title: Array Destruction and Spreading
docs.text:
• Destructuring is extracting array elements directly into variables.
  • list() is the old syntax and [] is the modern syntax.
<?php
// Modern Short Syntax (PHP 7.1+)
[$id, $name] = [101, 'Data Reader'];

// Legacy Equivalent (Very common in older code)
list($id, $name) = array(101, 'Data Reader');

// Keyed Destructuring (Extract specific keys from associative arrays)
['email' => $userEmail, 'role' => $userRole] = $user;
// $userEmail is now 'alex@example.com'
>
  • Array unpacking / spread operator (...) is used to expand an array inline or pass positional parameters into functions.
<?php
// 1. Merging Arrays (PHP 7.4+ for indexed, PHP 8.1+ for associative)
$baseRoles = ['user', 'editor'];
$allRoles  = [...$baseRoles, 'admin', 'superadmin'];
// Result: ['user', 'editor', 'admin', 'superadmin']

// 2. Variadic Functions (Unpacking parameters)
function executeQuery(string $sql, ...$params) {
    // $params inside the function is an array containing all extra arguments passed
}

$args = [42, 'active'];
executeQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? AND status = ?", ...$args);
// Expands to: executeQuery("...", 42, 'active')
>

docs.title: Essential Array Functions
docs.text:
• array_map(): Applies a callback function to every element and returns a new array of the exact same length. 
    <?php
$rawUserIds = ['1', '2', '3'];

// Convert array of string IDs to integers (Common during API query parsing)
$cleanIds = array_map(function($id) {
    return (int) $id;
}, $rawUserIds);
// Result: [1, 2, 3]
>

  • array_filter(): Iterates over elements and keeps only those where the callback returns true. 

    <?php
$rows = [
    ['id' => 1, 'deleted' => false],
    ['id' => 2, 'deleted' => true],
    ['id' => 3, 'deleted' => false]
];

// Strip out soft-deleted records
$activeRows = array_filter($rows, function($row) {
    return !$row['deleted'];
});
// this cannot make filtering decisions based on the keys
// PRESERVES original keys ([0 => row1, 2 => row3]).
// array_values() reset keys back to sequential [0, 1].
>

    • ARRAY_FILTER_USE_KEY modifies the behavior so that PHP passes only the array key into the callback function instead of the value. 

      <?php
$payload = [
    'username' => 'john_doe',
    'email'    => 'john@example.com',
    'is_admin' => 1 // <--- Malicious attempts to escalate privilege
];
$allowedColumns = ['username', 'email']; // Database columns allowed to be updated by this API endpoint

// Filter the payload by checking its KEYS against allowed columns
$safePayload = array_filter(
    $payload, 
    function($key) use ($allowedColumns) {
        // $key receives: 'username', 'email', 'is_admin'
        return in_array($key, $allowedColumns, true);
    }, 
    ARRAY_FILTER_USE_KEY // <--- Flag telling array_filter to pass keys to the callback
);

// Result of $safePayload:
// ['username' => 'john_doe', 'email' => 'john@example.com']
>

    • ARRAY_FILTER_USE_BOTH flag passes both the value and the key into the callback as two distinct arguments. 

      <?php
$data = [
    'first_name' => 'John',
    'last_name'  => '',
    'role'       => 'admin'
];

$result = array_filter(
    $data, 
    function($val, $key) {
        // Note the order: ($value, $key)
        // Keep only if the key doesn't start with 'last_' AND value is not empty
        return strpos($key, 'last_') !== 0 && $val !== '';
    }, 
    ARRAY_FILTER_USE_BOTH
);
>

    • array_reduce: Iterates through an array to reduce it down to a single output (e.g., building a SQL string or calculating a total). 
      <?php
$conditions = ['status = "active"', 'age > 18', 'role = "admin"'];

// Build a raw SQL WHERE clause
$whereClause = array_reduce($conditions, function($carry, $item) {
    return $carry === '' ? $item : $carry . ' AND ' . $item;
}, '');
// Result: 'status = "active" AND age > 18 AND role = "admin"'
>
    • array_merge(): Combines one or more arrays. 
      <?php
$defaults = ['status' => 'pending', 'limit' => 10];
$input    = ['limit' => 25, 'page' => 2];

$config = array_merge($defaults, $input);
// Result: ['status' => 'pending', 'limit' => 25, 'page' => 2]
// Rule: String keys in later arrays OVERWRITE earlier ones.
>
    • in_array(): Checks if a value exists inside an array. 
      <?php
if (in_array($requestedRole, ['admin', 'manager'])) {
    // Grant elevated access
}

// CRITICAL SAFETY WARNING: Loose vs Strict
in_array(0, ['admin', 'manager']);       // returns true in PHP 7.x due to loose comparison!
in_array(0, ['admin', 'manager'], true); // Third parameter enforcing strict check (===) returns false
>

docs.title: Control Structures
docs.text: Conditional execution structures dictate how request routing, feature flags, permissions, and database queries branching occur.

docs.title: Standard if / elseif / else
docs.text:
<?php
if ($user['role'] === 'admin') {
    $canAccess = true;
} elseif ($user['role'] === 'editor' && $isOwner) {
    $canAccess = true;
} else {
    $canAccess = false;
}
>

docs.title: Alternative Syntax (if ... : ... endif;)
docs.text:
<?php if ($user['status'] === 'active'): ?>
    <span class="badge active">Active User</span>
<?php elseif ($user['status'] === 'pending'): ?>
    <span class="badge pending">Pending Approval</span>
<?php else: ?>
    <span class="badge inactive">Disabled</span>
<?php endif; ?>

docs.title: Short Hand Conditionals
docs.text:
<?php
// Standard Ternary Operator
$page = isset($_GET['page']) ? (int)$_GET['page'] : 1;

// Shorthand Ternary
// If $_POST['title'] is empty string or unset, fallback to 'Untitled'
$title = $_POST['title'] ?: 'Untitled';

// Null Coalescing Operator (PHP 7.0+)
$limit = $_GET['limit'] ?? 20;
// Chaining null coalescing (reads left to right until first non-null)
$tenantId = $_GET['tenant_id'] ?? $_SESSION['tenant_id'] ?? 'default';

// Null Coalescing Assignment Operator (PHP 7.4+)
// Assigns the right side to the left variable only if the left variable is null or unassigned.
$config['db_port'] ??= 3306;
>

docs.title: switch Statement
docs.text:
• It is widely used in raw PHP REST API routers to execute different code depending on $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] or API action parameters.
  • A common source of legacy bugs is that switch checks cases using loose equality (==), NOT strict equality (===).
<?php
switch ($requestMethod) {
    case 'GET':
        $controller->index();
        break; // Crucial: Missing break results in fall-through!
    case 'POST':
        $controller->store();
        break;
    case 'PUT':
    case 'PATCH': // Intentional fall-through grouping multiple cases
        $controller->update();
        break;
    default:
        http_response_code(405);
        echo json_encode(['error' => 'Method Not Allowed']);
        break;
}

$action = 0; // Integer 0

switch ($action) {
    case 'edit': // PHP 7.x evaluates 0 == 'edit' is TRUE! during loose check
        echo "Performing Edit"; 
        break;
    case 0:
        echo "Performing Default Action";
        break;
}
>

docs.title: match Expression (PHP 8.0+)
The Standard PHP Hierarchy
docs.text:
interface Throwable
                       /                \
                      /                  \
        class Exception                   class Error
          /         \                     /         \
LogicException    RuntimeException    TypeError   ArithmeticError ...
  • Throwable is the top-level interface for everything that can be thrown via a throw statement.
  • Exception is the base class for application-level exceptions.
    • LogicException represents errors in code logic (e.g., InvalidArgumentException, DomainException).
    • RuntimeException represents errors that can only be detected at runtime (e.g., PDOException, OutOfBoundsException).
  • Error is the base class for internal PHP engine errors (e.g., TypeError, ParseError, DivisionByZeroError).

docs.title: Legacy error handling
docs.text: Before exceptions became standard, PHP relied on a legacy procedural error mechanism with different error levels (E_NOTICE, E_WARNING, E_DEPRECATED, E_ERROR).

docs.title: Custom Error Handlers (set_error_handler)
docs.text:
Raw PHP applications often register a global error handler in their entry file (index.php or bootstrap.php) to intercept traditional PHP warnings/notices and convert them into exceptions or JSON error responses.

<?php
// Converts standard PHP warnings/notices into thrown ErrorExceptions
set_error_handler(function (int $errno, string $errstr, string $errfile, int $errline) {
    // Don't execute handler if error reporting was disabled by the @ operator
    if (!(error_reporting() & $errno)) {
        return false;
    }

    // Convert the legacy error into a modern Exception
    throw new ErrorException($errstr, 0, $errno, $errfile, $errline);
});
>

docs.title: The Error Suppression Operator (@)
docs.text:
• The @ symbol placed before an expression instructs PHP to silently suppress any error, warning, or notice generated by that specific line.
  • Using @ forces PHP to dynamically alter error_reporting levels before and after evaluating the line, adding runtime overhead in hot loops.
  • Developers often use this to quickly hide "Undefined index" warnings. In doing so, they also hide database connection failures, file permission issues, or memory limit warnings, leading to silent failures downstream.
  • As of PHP 8.0, @ no longer hides fatal errors (like TypeError or ParseError). It only suppresses warnings and notices.
<?php
// Silently opens a file; if it fails, $file is false (no warning output)
$file = @fopen("non_existent_file.txt", "r");

// Silently attempts to parse an undefined array key
$value = @$data['missing_key'];
>

docs.title: Graceful Shutdown Handlers (register_shutdown_function)
docs.text:
• In raw REST APIs, if a script hits an uncatchable fatal error (like memory exhaustion), execution halts immediately.
  • Legacy apps use shutdown functions to output clean JSON instead of raw HTML error logs.
<?php
register_shutdown_function(function() {
    $error = error_get_last();
    if ($error !== null && in_array($error['type'], [E_ERROR, E_PARSE, E_COMPILE_ERROR])) {
        // Clear any output buffer already rendered
        if (ob_get_length()) {
            ob_clean();
        }

        http_response_code(500);
        echo json_encode([
            'status' => 'fatal_error',
            'message' => $error['message']
        ]);
    }
});
>

docs.title: Modern Exception Handling
docs.text:
• Since PHP 7.0, most internal engine errors (like passing invalid types, division by zero, or calling non-existent functions) were converted into Throwable objects.
  • This allows them to be caught using standard try-catch blocks instead of halting execution completely.
<?php
try {
    // Potentially dangerous code (e.g., parsing JSON, executing SQL)
    $data = json_decode($rawPayload, true, 512, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
    $result = $dbWrapper->insert($data);
} catch (JsonException $e) {
    // Triggered ONLY if JSON parsing fails
    http_response_code(400);
    echo json_encode(['error' => 'Malformed JSON: ' . $e->getMessage()]);
} catch (PDOException | QueryException $e) {
    // Multi-catch: Handles both PDO and custom ORM database exceptions
    http_response_code(500);
    echo json_encode(['error' => 'Database operation failed']);
} catch (Throwable $e) {
    // Global fallback catcher for ANY remaining exception or engine error
    http_response_code(500);
    echo json_encode(['error' => 'Unexpected error occurred']);
} finally {
    // ALWAYS executes regardless of whether an exception occurred or was caught
    // Used for cleanup: closing file handles, releasing locks, logging execution time
    $dbWrapper->releaseConnection();
}
>

docs.title: Object-Oriented PHP
docs.text: All content here was generated by Gemini.

docs.title: Object Allocation & References
docs.text:
• In PHP, objects are passed by handle (often referred to as passing by reference)
  • Though technically it is passing a copy of an object identifier value.
<?php
$user1 = new User("Alice");
$user2 = $user1;          // Both point to the same object instance
$user2->name = "Bob";     // Modifies $user1->name as well!

$user3 = clone $user1;    // Creates a shallow copy of the object
>

docs.title: Constructors & Property Promotion (PHP 8.0+)
docs.text:
• Legacy PHP uses explicit property declarations and manual assignment inside __construct().
  • Modern PHP codebases use Constructor Property Promotion, which combines parameter declaration and property assignment into one step.
<?php
// Modern Syntax (PHP 8.0+)
class User {
    public function __construct(
        public int $id,
        public string $name,
        private ?string $email = null
    ) {}
}

// Legacy Equivalent
class User {
    public int $id;
    public string $name;
    private ?string $email;

    public function __construct(int $id, string $name, ?string $email = null) {
        $this->id = $id;
        $this->name = $name;
        $this->email = $email;
    }
}
>

docs.title: Critical PHP Traps & Gotchas
docs.text:
• The $this Keyword
    • Unbound variables inside a method do not resolve to class properties.
    • $this->propertyName must be used explicitly to access an instance property.
    • Missing $this-> will look for a local variable instead.
  • Uninitialized Typed Properties
    • If a property has a type hint (e.g., public string $name;) and is accessed before assignment, PHP throws an Error: Typed property User::$name must not be accessed before initialization.
    • Use isset($this->name) to check initialization state safely.
  • Dynamic Properties (Deprecated in PHP 8.2+)
    • Historically, setting an undeclared property ($user->unknownProp = 10;) created a dynamic property on the fly.
    • In PHP 8.2+, this emits a deprecation warning unless the class uses the #[AllowDynamicProperties] attribute or implements __set().

docs.title: Visibility Modifiers
docs.text:
PHP enforces public, protected, and private at runtime.

Modifier Access from Current Class Access from Child Classes Access from Outside Instance public Yes Yes Yes protected Yes Yes No private Yes No No

docs.title: PHP-Specific Access Behaviors
docs.text:
• Default Visibility
    • If no modifier is specified on a method or property, PHP defaults it to public.
    • Best practice is explicit visibility.
  • Accessing Private Members Across Same-Class Instances
    • An instance of a class can access private properties of other instances of the exact same class.
    • This is frequently used in custom ORMs for cloning or merging model states.
  • Readonly Properties (PHP 8.1+)
    • Properties can be marked readonly.
    • They can only be initialized once (usually in the constructor) and cannot be modified afterward regardless of visibility.

docs.title: Static methods/properties
docs.text: Scope Keyword Meaning in PHP Syntax Example $this-> References the current object instance $this->name self:: References the class where the code is written self::$count static:: References the called class at runtime (Late Static Binding) static::find() parent:: References the parent class parent::__construct()

docs.title: Late Static Binding (self:: vs static::)
docs.text:
• When a parent base class (like BaseModel) provides static query methods (like User::find()), using self:: points to BaseModel, whereas static:: points to User.
<?php
abstract class BaseModel {
    public static function getTableNameSelf(): string {
        return self::$table; // Binds at compile-time to BaseModel
    }

    public static function getTableNameStatic(): string {
        return static::$table; // Binds at runtime to the calling child class
    }
}

class User extends BaseModel {
    protected static string $table = 'users';
}

// User::getTableNameSelf();   --> Error: Undefined static property BaseModel::$table
// User::getTableNameStatic(); --> Returns "users"
>

docs.title: Static Traps to Watch For
docs.text:
• Calling $this inside a static method throws an immediate Error: Using $this when not in object context.
  • Static properties are shared globally across all instances and requests within that worker process scope. They do not reset automatically between methods unless explicitly re-assigned.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
• Contain only public method signatures (and constant definitions).
  • Classes implement interfaces using implements InterfaceA, InterfaceB.
  • As of PHP 8.0, interfaces can define method parameters with type hints, union types, and return types that implementing classes must strictly match or widen.

docs.title: Abstract Classes
docs.text:
• Cannot be instantiated directly using new.
  • Can contain concrete methods with body logic, static methods, and properties alongside abstract method definitions.
  • Child classes extend abstract classes using extends ParentClass.
  • PHP supports single class inheritance only.

docs.title: Traits (Horizontal Code Reuse)
docs.text:
• Traits allow developers to inject reusable methods and properties into unrelated classes without using inheritance.
  • They are heavily used in custom ORMs for adding features like soft-deletes, timestamp tracking, or logging.
<?php
trait SoftDelete {
    protected ?string $deletedAt = null;

    public function delete(): void {
        $this->deletedAt = date('Y-m-d H:i:s');
        $this->save();
    }
}

class User extends BaseModel {
    use SoftDelete; // Injects $deletedAt property and delete() method into User
}

class Post extends BaseModel {
    use SoftDelete; // Reuses exact same logic in Post
}
>

docs.title: Gotchas with Traits
docs.text:
• Precedence Rules
    • Methods declared on the current class override Trait methods.
    • Trait methods override inherited methods from a parent class.
    • Precedence Order: Current Class Method > Trait Method > Extended Parent Method.
  • Naming Collisions
    • If two traits imported by the same class define a method with the exact same name, PHP throws a fatal compile error unless resolved using the insteadof operator: 
      <?php
class Product {
    use TraitA, TraitB {
        TraitA::log insteadof TraitB; // Explicitly pick TraitA's log method
    }
}
>

docs.title: Magic Methods
docs.text:
• These are reserved methods prefixed with two underscores (__).
  • They act as event hooks triggered automatically by the runtime in response to specific actions—such as accessing non-existent properties, calling missing methods, or serializing an object.

docs.title: __construct()
docs.text:
• Executes automatically when an object is instantiated via new.
  • Used for dependency injection, initializing model attributes, or opening database/file connections.

docs.title: __destruct()
docs.text:
• Executes automatically when no references to the object remain in memory, or during script shutdown.
  • Used for cleanups, closing database connections, flushing log buffers, or removing temporary locks.
  • It runs when memory is cleared by PHP's garbage collector.
  • If a script calls exit() or throws an uncaught exception, destructors still run during the shutdown phase, but their output buffers might already be closed.

docs.title: Property Interception
docs.text:
• In standard Active Record ORMs, database columns (e.g., email, created_at) are not hardcoded as explicit class properties.
  • Instead, they are stored internally in a key-value $attributes array.
  • When code accesses $user->email, PHP notices that $email is not declared on the class and automatically delegates the action to __get() and __set().
<?php
$user = new User();
$user->name = "Alice"; // Fires __set('name', 'Alice') -> populates $attributes['name']
echo $user->name;      // Fires __get('name')         -> returns $attributes['name']
>

docs.title: Dynamic Method Interception
docs.text:
• These methods allow classes to handle dynamic method invocations at runtime without defining dozens of concrete functions.
  • __call(string $name, array $arguments) is triggered when calling an inaccessible or non-existent instance method.
  • __callStatic(string $name, array $arguments) is triggered when calling an inaccessible or non-existent static method.
<?php
class User extends Model {
    public static function __callStatic(string $method, array $args): mixed {
        if (str_starts_with($method, 'findBy')) {
            $column = strtolower(substr($method, 6));
            $value  = $args[0] ?? null;
            return (new static())->where($column, '=', $value)->first();
        }
        throw new BadMethodCallException("Method {$method} does not exist.");
    }

    public function __call(string $method, array $args): mixed {
        return $this->newQueryBuilder()->$method(...$args);
    }
}

// Tracing execution:
$user = User::findByName("Alice"); 
// 1. PHP checks if User::findByName() exists. It doesn't.
// 2. PHP calls User::__callStatic('findByName', ['Alice']).
// 3. Method parses 'findByName' -> column 'name', executes SQL query automatically.
>

docs.title: Serialization and Type Casting
docs.text:
• When sending model instances over a REST API response, PHP needs to convert rich objects into formatted JSON payloads or string structures.
  • __toString() defines how an object behaves when cast to a string (e.g., echo $user; or (string)$user).
    • Must return a string and cannot throw uncaught exceptions in older PHP versions.
  • jsonSerialize() (JsonSerializable Interface)
    • While not an underscore magic method itself, JsonSerializable works hand-in-hand with json_encode().
    • When an object is passed into json_encode($user), PHP checks if it implements JsonSerializable.
    • If so, it invokes jsonSerialize() to extract serializable data.

docs.title: Namespaces & Autoloading
docs.text: • Modern and legacy raw PHP systems use namespaces to prevent class name collisions and Autoloaders to automatically locate and load file paths into memory on demand, instead of hundreds of manual require_once or include_once statements at the top of files.

docs.title: Namespace definitions and use imports
docs.text:
• Namespaces resolve class name conflicts by organizing code into logical directories/virtual modules, similar to packages in Java or namespaces in C#.
  • A namespace definition must be the very first statement in a PHP file (except for declare() statements).
  • Inside a declared namespace, PHP assumes any un-imported class belongs to the current namespace.
    • To call native PHP classes (like PDO, Exception, DateTime) or global legacy functions from inside a namespace, they must be prefixed with a leading backslash \ or imported with use.
  • When referencing a class defined in another namespace, it is imported using the use keyword.
  • PHP allows importing functions and constants directly using use function and use const.
<?php
namespace App\Models;

class User {
    // Fully Qualified Name (FQN): \App\Models\User
    // ERROR: PHP looks for \App\Models\PDO!
    $pdo = new PDO(...);

    // CORRECT: Leading \ instructs PHP to look in the Global Namespace
    $pdo = new \PDO(...);
}
>

<?php
namespace App\Controllers;

use App\Models\User;                    // Imports \App\Models\User
use App\Services\Auth\JWT as Tokenizer; // Class Aliasing
use function App\Helpers\format_date;
use const App\Config\MAX_RETRIES;

class AuthController {
    public function login(): void {
        $user = new User();              // Refers to \App\Models\User
        $token = Tokenizer::generate();  // Refers to \App\Services\Auth\JWT
    }
}
>

docs.title: Autoloading Mechanics
docs.text:
• It is the engine mechanism that eliminates manual require statements.
  • When PHP encounters a class that hasn't been defined yet (e.g., new User()), it triggers an autoload hook before throwing a "Class not found" error.
  • spl_autoload_register() is a native PHP function that registers custom callback functions to run whenever an unmapped class name is referenced.
<?php
spl_autoload_register(function (string $className) {
    // Convert namespace separators (\) to system directory separators (/)
    // App\Models\User -> App/Models/User
    $path = str_replace('\\', '/', $className);

    // Build full file path on disk
    $file = __DIR__ . '/src/' . $path . '.php';

    // Include the file if it exists
    if (file_exists($file)) {
        require_once $file;
    }
});

// When execution reaches this line:
$user = new \App\Models\User(); 
// PHP automatically passes 'App\Models\User' to the callback above!
>

docs.title: The PSR-4 Autoloading Standard
docs.text:
• PSR-4 (PHP Standard Recommendation 4) is the industry standard specification for mapping namespace prefixes to physical file directory paths.
  • The standard for autoloading is that an absolute class name takes the following form: $\(\text{\textbackslash NamespacePrefix\textbackslash SubNamespaces\textbackslash ClassName}\)$
  • A contiguous namespace prefix maps to a base directory on disk.
  • The sub-namespaces directly map to sub-directories underneath that base directory.
  • The class name maps strictly to ClassName.php (case-sensitive).

docs.title: Autoload Mapping
docs.text:
• Composer is frequently used solely as an autoloader and dependency manager.
  • It reads configuration settings inside composer.json to generate an optimized, high-performance autoloader script.
  • For Composer's autoloader to function, the main entry point file (index.php or bootstrap.php) requires a single file.
{
    "autoload": {
        "psr-4": {
            "App\\": "src/",
            "Database\\": "database/"
        },
        "files": [
            "src/Helpers/global_functions.php"
        ]
    }
}

<?php
// index.php

require_once __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

// Everything below this line is automatically loaded on demand!
$router = new \App\Core\Router();
$router->dispatch();
>

docs.title: REST API Architecture & Protocol
docs.text: All content here was generated by Gemini.

docs.title: Native Superglobals & HTTP Context
docs.text:
• In raw PHP REST APIs operating without web frameworks, there are no Request objects or abstractions wrapping HTTP requests.
  • The runtime relies entirely on PHP Superglobals (built-in global associative arrays provided by the PHP engine) for every incoming HTTP request.

docs.title: Reading Native Request Inputs
docs.text:
• PHP automatically populates specific superglobals based on the content type and HTTP method sent by the client.
  • $_GET parses URL query parameters (e.g., https://api.example.com/users?status=active&limit=10).
  • Despite its name, $_GET is populated for any HTTP request method that contains query parameters in the URL, including POST, PUT, or DELETE requests (e.g., POST /users?action=sync).
  • HTML Form Inputs: $_POST parses key-value body payloads only when the request uses POST and sets the Content-Type header to:
    • application/x-www-form-urlencoded
    • multipart/form-data
  • Request Server Environment: $_SERVER contains headers, paths, server configurations, and HTTP request context provided by the web server (Apache, Nginx, or Caddy).
<?php
// Request URL: /users?status=active&page=2
$status = $_GET['status'] ?? 'all';
$page   = isset($_GET['page']) ? (int)$_GET['page'] : 1;

// Handled automatically by PHP engine for form payloads
$username = $_POST['username'] ?? null;

// Extracting core request parameters
$httpMethod = $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'];                 // e.g., 'GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE'
$requestUri = $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'];                    // e.g., '/api/v1/users?id=10'
$clientIp   = $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'];                    // Originating IP address
$userAgent  = $_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] ?? 'Unknown';   // Client User-Agent string
>

docs.title: Parsing non-POST payloads
docs.text:
• Modern REST APIs send JSON payloads (Content-Type: application/json) using verbs like POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE.
  • PHP's $_POST superglobal is completely empty when receiving application/json payloads or non-POST requests (PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
  • To read raw HTTP request bodies, custom API controllers read the php://input stream directly.

  • php://input is a read-only stream that yields the raw bytes from the HTTP request body.

    <?php
// Read the raw HTTP request body string
$rawPayload = file_get_contents('php://input');

// Parse JSON into an associative array ($assoc = true)
$data = json_decode($rawPayload, true);

// Check for JSON parsing errors
if (json_last_error() !== JSON_ERROR_NONE) {
    http_response_code(400);
    echo json_encode([
        'error' => 'Invalid JSON payload',
        'details' => json_last_error_msg()
    ]);
    exit;
}

// $data is now a standard PHP associative array ready for use
$email = $data['email'] ?? null;
>

  • php://input cannot be read more than once in SAPI environments with enctype="multipart/form-data".

  • Reading file_get_contents('php://input') pulls the entire payload into RAM.
  • For API endpoints expecting large file uploads via REST, raw PHP code uses fopen('php://input', 'rb') to stream data in chunks rather than buffering the entire payload into memory.

docs.title: Parsing Request Headers
docs.text: • HTTP request headers provide authentication tokens (Authorization), payload metadata (Content-Type), and client context.

docs.title: Standard Method (getallheaders())
docs.text:
• In web server environments (Apache, Nginx with FPM), getallheaders() returns an associative array of all client HTTP headers. 
    <?php
$headers = getallheaders();
// Accessing specific headers (Note: Header keys can vary in casing depending on server)
$authHeader = $headers['Authorization'] ?? $headers['authorization'] ?? null;
>

docs.title: Fallback Server Extraction via $_SERVER
docs.text:
• If running under specific CGI/SAPI environments where getallheaders() is unavailable, custom APIs extract headers directly from $_SERVER.
  • PHP automatically converts incoming request headers in $_SERVER using three rules:
    • Prefixes the header name with HTTP_.
    • Converts all letters to uppercase.
    • Replaces dashes (-) with underscores (_).
  • So, X-Api-Key becomes $_SERVER['HTTP_X_API_KEY']

docs.title: Custom API Routing & Request Handling
docs.text:
• In a raw PHP REST API, there is no framework router to automatically dispatch incoming requests.
  • Architecture relies on web server URL rewrites to route all traffic to a single entry file (index.php), where custom script logic parses the URI and dispatches requests.

docs.title: Web Server URL Rewriting (Front Controller Pattern)
docs.text: • To enable clean REST endpoints (like /api/users/42 instead of index.php?controller=users&id=42), the web server redirects all incoming HTTP requests to index.php unless a physical file or directory matches the request path.

docs.title: Apache Rewrite Configuration
docs.text:
• .htaccess file is placed in the web root directory alongside index.php.
  • Query String Append (QSA) preserves URL parameters (e.g., /api/users?page=2 retains ?page=2 inside $_GET).
  • By default, Apache strips the Authorization header (HTTP_AUTHORIZATION) when forwarding requests to PHP CGI/FPM process pools. This explicit rule preserves Bearer tokens for authentication handlers.
<?php
# .htaccess file
RewriteEngine On

# Pass Authorization header to PHP CGI/FastCGI environments
RewriteRule .* - [E=HTTP_AUTHORIZATION:%{HTTP:Authorization}]

# If the requested file or directory physically exists, serve it directly
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d

# Otherwise, rewrite all traffic to index.php
RewriteRule ^ index.php [QSA,L]
>

docs.title: Custom URI Parsing and Route Dispatching
docs.text: • Once execution reaches index.php, the router extracts the URI path and matches it against registered endpoints.

docs.title: Simple Switch/Method Dispatching (Legacy Style)
docs.text:
<?php
$method = $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'];
$uri    = parse_url($_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'], PHP_URL_PATH);

// Strip base subdirectories if API resides under /api/v1
$uri = str_replace('/api/v1', '', $uri);

switch ($uri) {
    case '/users':
        if ($method === 'GET') $controller->listUsers();
        elseif ($method === 'POST') $controller->createUser();
        break;

    case '/health':
        echo json_encode(['status' => 'OK']);
        break;

    default:
        http_response_code(404);
        echo json_encode(['error' => 'Endpoint Not Found']);
        break;
}
>

docs.title: Regex Dynamic Routing
docs.text:
• Supports dynamic route variables (e.g., /users/{id} or /orders/{id}/items).
<?php
class Router {
    private array $routes = [];

    public function add(string $method, string $pathPattern, callable|array $handler): void {
        // Convert route pattern /users/{id} into regex pattern ^/users/([^/]+)$
        $regex = preg_replace('/\{([a-zA-Z0-9_]+)\}/', '([^/]+)', $pathPattern);
        $regex = '#^' . $regex . '$#';

        $this->routes[] = [
            'method'  => strtoupper($method),
            'regex'   => $regex,
            'handler' => $handler
        ];
    }

    public function dispatch(string $requestMethod, string $requestUri): void {
        $path = parse_url($requestUri, PHP_URL_PATH);

        foreach ($this->routes as $route) {
            if ($route['method'] !== $requestMethod) {
                continue;
            }

            if (preg_match($route['regex'], $path, $matches)) {
                array_shift($matches); // Remove full match from captures

                $handler = $route['handler'];
                if (is_array($handler)) {
                    [$class, $method] = $handler;
                    call_user_func_array([new $class(), $method], $matches);
                } else {
                    call_user_func_array($handler, $matches);
                }
                return;
            }
        }

        http_response_code(404);
        echo json_encode(['error' => 'Route not found']);
    }
}
>

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes & Response Headers
docs.text:
• To return a valid REST API response, PHP must emit both an HTTP status code and an explicit Content-Type header before sending any output bytes to the client.

  • Setting Response Status Codes

    • Native function http_response_code(int $code) gets or sets the HTTP response status code.
    // Sets the HTTP status to 201 Created
http_response_code(201);

// Reads the current status code back
$currentStatus = http_response_code(); // Returns 201

  • Setting Response Headers

    • The header(string $header, bool $replace = true, int $response_code = 0) function sends raw HTTP headers directly to the web server/client.
    // Explicitly notify client payload is JSON formatted
header('Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8');

// Prevent client/proxy caching for dynamic API endpoints
header('Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate');

// CORS / Security headers
header('X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff');

  • HTTP headers and status codes must be sent before any response content body (HTML, whitespace, or BOM markers) is output.

  • Otherwise, it will triggers PHP warning "Cannot modify header information - headers already sent"
  • To prevent this in custom frameworks, APIs often use Output Buffering at entry points.

docs.title: Data Serialization with json_encode()
docs.text:
• json_encode(mixed $value, int $flags = 0, int $depth = 512) converts PHP data structures (arrays, scalar primitives, objects) into JSON formatted strings.
  • Modern and legacy raw PHP applications pass bitmask flags into json_encode() to alter output format and safety parameters.
  • JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES: Prevents escaping / as \/ (keeps URLs readable).
  • JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE: Encodes multibyte UTF-8 characters natively instead of converting them to unicode escape sequences like \u00e0.
  • JSON_NUMERIC_CHECK: Forces stringified numbers ("100") to serialize as native numeric types (100). This can convert string phone numbers or ZIP codes like "01234" to integers, stripping leading zeros.
  • JSON_PRETTY_PRINT: Formats output with indentation whitespace for visual debugging.
  • JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR (PHP 7.3+): Instructs json_encode() or json_decode() to throw a JsonException upon failure rather than returning false.
$data = [
    'id' => 42,
    'title' => 'API Guide & Tips',
    'url' => 'https://example.com/api?user=1&type=test',
    'amount' => 1250.50
];

// Standard Production REST Encoding
echo json_encode($data, JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE);
// Output: {"id":42,"title":"API Guide & Tips","url":"https://example.com/api?user=1&type=test","amount":1250.5}

// Development / Debug Pretty Printing
echo json_encode($data, JSON_PRETTY_PRINT);

docs.title: Handling JSON Serialization Errors
docs.text:
• By default, if json_encode() fails, it returns false silently.
  • Outputting false directly results in an empty response body sent to the client, even if HTTP 200 OK status was declared.
  • json_last_error() is used in legacy PHP to check for errors.
  • Common Error Codes returned by json_last_error():
    • JSON_ERROR_DEPTH: Exceeded maximum stack depth (default 512).
    • JSON_ERROR_STATE_MISMATCH: Invalid or malformed JSON state.
    • JSON_ERROR_CTRL_CHAR: Unexpected control character found.
    • JSON_ERROR_UTF8: Malformed UTF-8 characters. Extremely common when pulling raw legacy MySQL database columns saved in non-UTF8 character sets like latin1.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• A popular open-source build tool developed by the Apache Group to build, publish, and deploy several projects.
  • A robust project management tool based on the POM architecture.
  • It simplifies the day-to-day work of Java developers and aids in the comprehension of any Java-based project.
  • It takes care of Builds, Dependencies, Reports, Distribution, Releases, Mailing list, Documentation, SCMs.
  • Can also be used to create and manage projects written in other languages such as C#, Ruby, Scala.
  • Use variations of Maven (e.g. Polyglot Maven), or Maven Plugins to use other languages than JAVA.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Making the build process easy
  • Providing a uniform build system
  • Providing quality project information
  • Encouraging better development practices
  • While using Maven doesn't eliminate the need to know about the underlying mechanisms, Maven does shield developers from many details.
  • Maven builds a project using its project object model (POM) and a set of plugins. Once you familiarize yourself with one Maven project, you know how all Maven projects build. This saves time when navigating many projects.
  • Maven provides useful project information that is in part taken from your POM and in part generated from your project's sources. For example, Maven can provide:
    • Change log created directly from source control
    • Cross referenced sources
    • Mailing lists managed by the project
    • Dependencies used by the project
    • Unit test reports including coverage
  • Third party code analysis products also provide Maven plugins that add their reports to the standard information given by Maven.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• Environment Variables
    • MAVEN OPTS contains parameters used to start up the JVM running Maven and can be used to supply additional options to it.
    • MAVEN ARGS contains arguments passed to Maven before CLI arguments.
  • settings.xml, located in USER HOME/.m2 the settings files is designed to contain any configuration for Maven usage across projects.
  • .mvn, files in this directory contain project specific configuration for running Maven.
  • maven.config is used to specify command-line options for Maven at the project level. This allows to configure global options that should apply whenever Maven commands are run within the project.
  • jvm.config lets define JVM configuration, i.e. define the options for the build on a per project base.
  • extensions.xml is used to configure Maven core extensions. These extensions are automatically included when anyone builds the project.

docs.title: .mvn/extensions.xml file
docs.text: Previously, it was very painful to change maven installation, or extend it. This file helps to do this easily.

docs.title: .mvn/maven.config file
docs.text: It was really hard to define a general set of options for calling the maven command line. This file makes it easier on a per-project basis.

docs.title: .mvn/jvm.config file
docs.text:
For example if we put the following JVM options into the .mvn/jvm.config file 

-Xmx2048m -Xms1024m -XX:MaxPermSize=512m -Djava.awt.headless=true
we don't need to use these options in MAVEN_OPTS or switch between different configurations.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Maven’s architecture revolves around the concept of Project Object Model (POM), which serves as the blueprint for managing the build process.
  • This works in three steps:
    1. Read the pom.xml file.
    2. Download the dependencies defined in pom.xml into the local repository from the central repository.
    3. Create and generate a report according to the requirements, and executes life-cycles, phases, goals, plugins, etc.

Maven Architecture

docs.title: Project Object Model (POM)
docs.text:
• Refers to the XML files with all the information regarding project and configuration details.
  • Central piece of Maven’s architecture. It defines the project’s structure, dependencies, build configuration, and other project-related information.
  • Included in the POM: Dependencies, Developers and contributors, Plugins, Plugin configuration, Resources.
  • The XML file is in the project home directory. When we tend to execute a task, Maven searches for the POM in the current directory.

docs.title: Minimum required elements for POM
docs.text:
• project - The root element of the pom.xml file.
  • modelVersion – identifies which version of the POM model you’re working with. For Maven 2 and Maven 3, use version 4.0.0.
  • groupId – Project group’s identifier. It is unique, and you will most likely use a group ID that is similar to the project’s root Java package name.
  • artifactId – Used for naming the project you’re working on.
  • version – The version number of the project is contained in the version element. If your project has been released in multiple versions, it is helpful to list the versions.

docs.title: Maven coordinates
docs.text:
• Uniquely identify a project, a dependency, or a plugin defined in POM.
  • Each entity is uniquely identified by the combination of a group identifier (groupId element), an artifact identifier (artifactId element), and the version (version element).
  • The groupId and the version elements can also be inherited from the parent POM file.

docs.title: Pre-defined properties
docs.text:
• Can be used to simplify and manage build configuration more effectively.
  • These properties are automatically available in the pom.xml and can be referenced using the $propertyName syntax.

docs.title: Project Properties
docs.text:
• Provide information about the current project.
  • $project.groupId: The group ID of the project.
  • $project.artifactId: The artifact ID of the project.
  • $project.version: The version of the project.
  • $project.packaging: The packaging type of the project (e.g., jar, war).

docs.title: Build Properties
docs.text:
• Provide information about the build configuration.
  • $project.build.directory: The directory where the build output is generated.
  • $project.build.outputDirectory: The directory where compiled classes are placed.
  • $project.build.finalName: The final name of the built artifact without the extension.

docs.title: User Properties
docs.text:
• Refer to settings specific to the user running Maven, typically defined in the settings.xml file.
  • Example:
    • $user.home -> The user's home directory
    • $user.name -> The user's login name

docs.title: Environment Properties
docs.text:
• Allow access to environment variables defined in the operating system.
  • $env.VAR NAME, where VAR NAME is the name of the environment variable.

docs.title: System Properties
docs.text:
• Are Java system properties that can be accessed during the build.
  • $java.version: The version of the Java runtime environment.
  • $os.name: The name of the operating system.

docs.title: Maven Properties
docs.text:
• Are specific to Maven itself.
  • $maven.version: The version of Maven being used.
  • $maven.home: The installation directory of Maven.
  • $maven.repo.local: The path to the local Maven repository.

docs.title: User-defined properties
docs.text:
• These properties can be referenced in Maven just like any other property, i.e. $arbitrary.property.
  • Can be created in the POM as follows:
<properties>
    <arbitrary.property>Text</arbitrary.property>
</properties>

docs.title: Benefits of Using Properties
docs.text:
• Centralized Configuration: Properties allows to define values in a single location, and makes it easier to manage and update configuration values.
  • Reusability: Properties can be reused across multiple places in the pom.xml, reducing redundancy.
  • Maintainability: Centralizing values makes it easier to update them.
  • Flexibility: Different values can be injected at build time using profiles, system properties, or environment variables.
  • Customization: Allows for customization of builds for different environments (development, testing, production) using profiles.

docs.title: Super POM
docs.text:
• A part of the Maven installation, and refers to the default POM of Maven.
  • All Maven project POMs extend the Super POM, which defines a set of defaults shared by all projects.
  • All of the configurations defined in the super POM file is inherited by even the simplest version of a POM file.
  • Options of super POM can be altered by redefining that same section.
  • To execute any particular objectives, effective POM is used.

POM Hierarchy

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• A dependency in Maven refers to an external library or module that a project needs in order to compile, build, and run.
  • Used to include reusable code from third-party libraries, frameworks, or other projects, avoiding the need to write everything from scratch.
  • They help in modularizing the code, improving code reuse, and managing library versions.
  • Maven automates the process of downloading, linking, and updating dependencies, which ensures that the project always uses the correct versions of libraries.

docs.title: System Dependency
docs.text:
• Refers to the dependency that is present with the scope system.
  • These dependencies are commonly used to help Maven know the dependencies that are provided by the JDK or VM.
  • Mostly used to resolve dependencies on artifacts that are provided by the JDK.
  • Some common examples are the Java Authentication and Authorization Service (JAAS) or the JDBC standard extensions.

docs.title: Transitive dependencies
docs.text:
• Indirect dependencies that a project inherits from its direct dependencies.
  • When a project depends on a library, and that library depends on other libraries, Maven automatically includes those additional libraries in the project.
  • Example: If your project depends on Library A, and Library A depends on Library B, Maven will include Library B automatically.
  • Although transitive dependencies can implicitly include desired dependencies, it is a good practice to explicitly specify the dependencies your source code uses directly.

docs.title: Dependency Mediation
docs.text:
• This determines what version of an artifact will be chosen when multiple versions are encountered as dependencies.
  • Maven picks the ”nearest definition”, i.e., it uses the version of the closest dependency to the project in the tree of dependencies.
  • It can always be guaranteed a version by declaring it explicitly in the project’s POM.
  • If two dependency versions are at the same depth in the dependency tree, the first declaration wins.

Maven Dependency Mediation

docs.title: Dependency management
docs.text:
• Allows project authors to declare the versions of artifacts that are to be utilized when they are discovered in transitive dependencies or dependencies that have no version specified.
  • Ensures consistent dependency versions across multiple modules in a project.

docs.title: Specifying Dependencies in pom.xml using dependencies tag
docs.text:
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-core</artifactId>
        <version>5.3.8</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

docs.title: Specifying Dependencies in pom.xml using dependencyManagement tag
docs.text:
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
            <artifactId>commons-lang3</artifactId>
            <version>3.14.0</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

docs.title: Dependency Scope
docs.text:
• The scope of a dependency determines when the dependency is required and available during the build lifecycle.
  • There are 6 scopes:
    • compile: Default scope, required for all phases of the project lifecycle. 
      <scope>compile</scope>
    • test: Used only during the testing phase. 
      <scope>test</scope>
    • provided: Required for compilation but not packaged in the WAR/JAR. It’s provided by the runtime environment. 
      <scope>provided</scope>
    • runtime: Not needed for compilation but required for execution. 
      <scope>runtime</scope>
    • system: Similar to provided, but you must explicitly provide the JAR file on your system. 
      <scope>system</scope>
<systemPath>${project.basedir}/lib/my-library.jar</systemPath>
    • import: Only supported in the <dependencyManagement> section. It indicates the dependency is to be replaced with the effective list of dependencies in the specified POM’s <dependencyManagement> section. Since they are replaced, dependencies with a scope of import do not actually participate in limiting the transitivity of a dependency.

docs.title: Optional Dependency
docs.text:
• Used when a library (or module) includes other libraries that are not necessarily required by every project using the library.
  • They help avoid pulling in transitive dependencies that are not always needed, preventing unnecessary bloat and potential conflicts in dependent projects.
  • Used when it’s not possible to split a project into sub-modules.
  • They save storage and memory.
  • They prevent troublesome jars from being packed into a WAR, JAR, or other formats, if they violate a license agreement or cause classpath difficulties.
  • Include <optional>true</optional> inside a package’s dependency declaration to make it optional.

docs.title: Dependency Exclusions
docs.text:
• Since Maven resolves dependencies transitively, it is possible for unwanted dependencies to be included in a project’s classpath.
  • Maven allows excluding such dependencies.
  • Exclusions are set on a specific dependency in the POM, and are targeted at a specific groupId and artifactId.
  • When the project is built, that artifact will not be added to the project’s classpath.

Defining Dependency Exclusions in pom.xml

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.hibernate</groupId>
    <artifactId>hibernate-core</artifactId>
    <version>5.4.0.Final</version>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.jboss.logging</groupId>
            <artifactId>jboss-logging</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

Why exclusions are made on a per-dependency basis, rather than at the POM level? This is mainly to be sure the dependency graph is predictable, and to keep inheritance effects from excluding a dependency that should not be excluded. If you get to the method of last resort and have to put in an exclusion, you should be absolutely certain which of your dependencies is bringing in that unwanted transitive dependency. If you truly want to ensure that a particular dependency appears nowhere in your classpath, regardless of path, the banned dependencies rule can be configured to fail the build if a problematic dependency is found. When the build fails, you'll need to add specific exclusions on each path the enforcer finds.

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text:
• Refer to the directories of packaged JAR files that contain metadata.
  • The metadata refers to the POM files relevant to each project.
  • This metadata is what allows Maven to download dependencies.
  • If the dependencies are not present in the local repository, then Maven downloads them from a central repository and stores them in the local repository. to download dependencies.

docs.title: Local Repository
docs.text:
• Refers to the machine of the developer where all the project material is saved, and contains all the dependency jars.
  • Maven saves all of the JARs, dependency files, and other things it downloads in the Maven local repository.
  • All of the artifacts are kept locally in the Maven local repository, which is a folder on the local machine.
  • To manually install the JAR into the local Maven repository: install-file-Dfile = <file path>.

docs.title: Remote Repositories
docs.text:
• Refers to the repository present on a server (e.g. Maven Central) that is used when Maven needs to download dependencies.
  • Whenever anything is required from the remote repository, it is first downloaded to the local repository, and then it is used.
  • Central Repository, also known as Maven Central, is the default remote repository that Maven queries to download dependencies.

docs.title: Custom Repository
docs.text:
• Refers to user-defined repositories, either remote or internal, specified in the POM file or settings.
  • Used to
    • host proprietary or internal artifacts not suitable for public distribution.
    • centralize dependencies and artifacts specific to an organization.

docs.title: Repository Configuration
docs.text:
in pom.xml

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>my-private-repo</id>
        <url>http://repo.mycompany.com/maven2</url>
        <releases>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
        </releases>
        <snapshots>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
        </snapshots>
    </repository>
</repositories>

in settings.xml

<profiles>
    <profile>
    <id>custom-repo-profile</id>
    <repositories>
        <repository>
        <id>my-private-repo</id>
        <url>http://repo.mycompany.com/maven2</url>
        <releases>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
        </releases>
        <snapshots>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
        </snapshots>
        </repository>
    </repositories>
    </profile>
</profiles>

<activeProfiles>
    <activeProfile>custom-repo-profile</activeProfile>
</activeProfiles>
settings.xml can be customized for both Global Settings and User Settings.

docs.title: Dependency Resolution Process
docs.text:
• Check Local Repository: Maven looks for the dependency in the local cache (~/.m2/repository).
  • Check Custom Repositories: If not found locally, Maven checks the custom repositories listed in the <repositories> section of the pom.xml.
  • Check Central Repository: If the dependency is still not found, Maven checks the central repository.

docs.title: Repository Order
docs.text:
• Remote repository URLs are queried in the following order for artifacts until one returns a valid result:
    1. Effective settings:
      • Global settings.xml
      • User settings.xml
    2. Local effective build POM:
      • Local pom.xml
      • Parent POMs, recursively
      • Super POM
    3. Effective POMs from dependency path to the artifact.

docs.title: Plugin
docs.text:
• Refers to collections of goals that can be executed during the build process.
  • Are essential features of Maven that are used to reuse the common build logic across several projects.
  • Used to:
    • Create a JAR/WAR file.
    • Compile code files.
    • Unit testing of code.
    • Create project documentation.
    • Create project reports.
  • There are two types of Maven Plugins:
    • Build plugins are executed during the build and are configured in the <build/> element of pom.xml.
    • Reporting plugins are executed during the stage generation and are configured in the <reporting/> element of the pom.xml.

docs.title: How Plugins Work?
docs.text:
• By defining goals, which are specific tasks that the plugin can perform.
  • When a Maven build is run, user specifies which goals to be execute.
  • For example, running mvn clean compile will execute the clean goal from the maven-clean-plugin and the compile goal from the maven-compiler-plugin.

docs.title: Configuring Plugins in pom.xml
docs.text:
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>3.8.1</version>
            <configuration>
                <source>1.8</source>
                <target>1.8</target>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

docs.title: Lifecycle Integration
docs.text:
• If the plugin is included in the pom.xml, it will be executed automatically during the build phases.
  • For example, the compile goal of the maven-compiler-plugin is bound to the compile phase of the default lifecycle.

docs.title: Commonly Used Plugins
docs.text:
• Clean plugin cleans the project by removing files generated at build time.
  • Install plugin installs the project’s artifact into the local repository.
  • Deploy plugin deploys the artifact to a remote repository.
  • Surefire Plugin runs an application’s unit tests during the test phase of the build lifecycle. It can generate reports in one of two file formats: plain text files or XML files.

docs.title: Custom Plugins
docs.text:
• If users’ build process involves tasks that are not covered by existing plugins, a custom plugin can fill that gap.
  • Helps to automate repetitive tasks specific to your development process.
  • To create a custom Maven plugin
    • Create a new Maven project with the appropriate structure.
    • Create a Java class that extends AbstractMojo from the Maven Plugin API, and implement the logic for the plugin within this class.
    • Use the plugin.xml file to define the plugin’s metadata and goals.
    • Build the custom plugin with mvn package.
@Mojo(name = "sayhi", defaultPhase = LifecyclePhase.COMPILE)
public class GreetingMojo extends AbstractMojo {
    @Parameter(property = "sayhi.greeting", defaultValue = "Hello, World!")
    private String greeting;
    public void execute() throws MojoExecutionException {
        getLog().info(greeting);
    }
}

docs.title: MOJO
docs.text:
• Can be defined as a Maven plain Old Java Object.
  • Every MOJO is an executable goal in Maven, and a plugin refers to the distribution of such MOJOs.
  • Enables Maven to extend the functionality that is already not found in it.
  • Can be executed at different phases of the Maven build lifecycle, such as compile, test, package, install, and deploy.

docs.title: Build Lifecycle
docs.text:
• A sequence of phases that define the order in which goals are executed during the build process.
  • Built-in build lifecycles
    • Default Lifecycle: Handles the project deployment, covering tasks such as compilation, testing, packaging, and deployment.
    • Clean Lifecycle: Handles project cleaning, which involves removing files generated by the previous build.
    • Site Lifecycle: Handles the creation of project documentation and reports.
  • Each lifecycle is made up of a series of phases, and each phase can be associated with one or more plugin goals.

Maven Build Life Cycle

docs.title: Binding Goals to Phases
docs.text:
• Goals are bound to phases either by default or by explicit configuration in the pom.xml.
  • For example: The maven-compiler-plugin:compile goal is bound to the compile phase by default.

Explicitly bind goals to phases

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>3.8.1</version>
            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <phase>compile</phase>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>compile</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
